newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Brazil's Garantia sees tough competition.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brazil's Garantia sees tough competition.

text.p: Brazilian investment banks, whose earnings have soared under two years of economic stabilization, face tougher times due to stiffer competition and prospects of falling profit margins, Banco de Investimentos Garantia executive Claudio Haddad said.

"Investment banks have prospered and thrived under stabilization. But I think if you look ahead ... competition will become much stronger and there will be a consolidation process," Haddad told Reuters in an interveiw.

Brazil's economic opening over the past five years created a huge demand for the underwriting of debt and equity securities and assistance with corporate restructurings, mergers and acquisitions, Haddad said.

In addition, a tight monetary policy anchoring Brazil's 27-month-old stabilization drive has maintained a strong local currency and high interest rates, which has attracted billions of foreign dollars into the fixed-income portfolios of Garantia and other Brazilian investment banks.

The promising business has led foreign investment banks like Merrill Lynch, Salomon Brothers, Oppenheimer & Co and others to open offices or expand existing operations in Brazil over the past two years.
The growth in Garantia's net profits over the past few years illustrates the attraction.

In 1994, the first year of Brazil's anti-inflationary Real Plan, Garantia's earnings totalled about $73 million. Garantia profits jumped 43 percent to $105 million in 1995 and the bank is expected to post a $120 million profit this year, Haddad said.
But the spread between Brazilian and global interest rates has fallen sharply over the past 10 months, cutting into fixed-income gains and slowing the net flow of dollars to Brazil.
"We can envision that spreads are going to fall further so I think that there is going to be a consolidation of the investment banking sector," Haddad said.
Although it will become harder for investment banks to make money in Brazil, Haddad said there would still be plenty of business in the area of corporate finance.
He noted that foreign companies were increasingly interested in acquiring Brazilian firms to gain a slice of market share in Latin America's largest economy.
"Foreign companies are increasingly attracted. They are looking at Brazil and seeing stability and seeing that it is moving in the right direction," Haddad said.
Colgate-Palmolive, Unilever and other multinationals have already acquired stakes in Brazilian firms and Haddad said the trend would continue.
Garantia, the leader in mergers and acquisitions in Brazil, was the sole Brazilian adviser on Colgate-Palmolive's $1.0 billion acquisition of Brazil's Anakol and its Kolynos toothpaste brand.
Project finance, once thought to be a promising sector in Brazil, would remain a small part of Garantia's business, Haddad said.

"This is still an undeveloped sector. There are a lot of problems with it because it is a long-term investment based on flows and results generated by the project. Given our short history of stability, there are risks involved," he said.
